extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent agents, and lawyers seeking practical guidance on patentability under (historical) UK patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what subject-matter is legally patentable (and what is not), the substantive requirements for a valid patent (utility, novelty, ingenuity, first inventor, sufficiency of specification), and the principal classes of inventions and examples used by the courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: referable to a 'manner of manufacture' (statute of James I)
rubrics_metrics.description: No invention is patentable which does not fall within the language of the Act of King James, and is not referable to some 'manner of new manufactures.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The words have been given a wide interpretation, but do not include an abstract principle without practical application, a game of skill or chance irrespective of appliances, a method of calculation without apparatus, a vegetable suitable for food, a natural substance applicable to a useful purpose (e.g. guano), or an elementary body such as a metal — unless taken out for the manufacture of apparatus required for the purpose or methods of preparing the natural substance for some useful end. Quote: 'No invention is patentable which does not fall within the language of the Act of King James, and is not referable to some 'manner of new manufactures.''

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive invention requirements: utility, novelty, and ingenuity
rubrics_metrics.description: In order that a patent should be held valid in a court of law the invention must possess a certain amount of utility; must display some degree of novelty; and must have been attained by the exercise of some measure of ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three elements are presented as cumulative prerequisites to sustain a patent under legal scrutiny. (This is given as an explicit three-point test in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship/origination: true and first inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must be the true and first inventor; he must not have obtained the invention from another person (unless he has imported it from abroad); nor must he have derived it from a printed book or from a patent specification published in this country or introduced from abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing first invention/original derivation is a substantive bar to validity; prior public disclosure or derivation defeats novelty and inventorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirements: accuracy, intelligibility, sufficiency, and distinct claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification, that is the patentee's formal description of his invention, must be accurate, intelligible, and sufficient; it must point out distinctly what the patentee claims as his own; and must not claim anything that is not his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly stresses that the specification must describe how to carry the invention into effect (mode/embodiment) and must clearly delimit the patentee's monopoly; deficiencies in specification (vagueness, over-claiming) will jeopardize validity. See also guidance that one should consult an experienced practitioner rather than rely solely on books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bare principles and abstract discoveries are not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Bare principles are not patentable. A principle, however valuable to philosophers, if not shown to have at least one application to a useful purpose (means of gaining an immediate material advantage), is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts state that a patent cannot be taken out 'for a mere principle' — it must be embodied in a concrete form and application. Quoted judicial formulations: 'You cannot take out a patent for a principle. You may take out a patent for a principle coupled with the mode of carrying the principle into effect...' and 'it is not a patent for a mere principle; but for a principle so far embodied and connected with corporeal substances as to be in a condition to act and to produce effects...'. Examples: Watt's steam-condensing invention was acceptable because Watt 'carried that practically into effect by describing a mode which would effect the object.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Must disclose a mode of carrying a principle into effect (embodiment requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be supported, a patent claiming the application of a principle must include an embodiment — a practical mode described in the specification for carrying the principle into effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts reject claims that amount to asserting 'every shape' or claiming a principle in the abstract. The specification must 'start with having invented some mode of carrying the principle into effect.' Example: Neilson's patent succeeded because he claimed a mode embodied in apparatus (an air-vessel) rather than a mere principle; conversely, claiming 'every shape' of vessel would be a claim to principle and invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes/methods can be patentable (broad interpretation of 'manufacture')
rubrics_metrics.description: A process or method may be patentable; the word 'manufacture' has been given a large interpretation to include the practice of making, principles carried into practice, and new modes producing new results or producing known substances in a new or better way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although initially doubted, authorities and cases (e.g., Gibson v. Brand, Boulton v. Bull) recognize that processes — including methods producing known substances more cheaply or efficiently, or new methods of applying known materials — fall within the statute. Examples include methods for manufacturing silk, producing gas by direct distillation of seeds, and duplicate signalling methods in telegraphy. The treatise explains that the real invention may be the mode of production rather than the product itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes of patentable inventions (illustrative taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions for which valid patents have been granted may be roughly divided into classes: (1) new contrivances applied to new objects/purposes producing new results; (2) new contrivances applied to old objects/purposes; (3) new combinations of old parts or of old parts and new parts, or material/technical processes; (4) new methods of applying a known thing; (5) chemical processes, sometimes combined with machinery or contrivances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual supplies multiple examples for each class (electric telegraphy, telephonic apparatus, photography, electroplating for class 1; application of old contrivance to known ends for class 2; combinations like hot-air blast with anthracite for class 3; modes of applying known materials for class 4; and chemical processes for class 5). This taxonomy is intended as practical guidance on the types of inventions the courts have upheld.

rubrics_metrics.name: New combination of known parts/processes is patentable if it yields a substantial improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A new combination of known parts, or of old parts and old processes producing a new result, or producing an old result more economically or in better form, will be held patentable if the combination constitutes a substantial improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial authority supports patents where combination of previously known elements produces utility/advantage making the combination a 'substantial improvement' (e.g., Crane v. Price: hot-air blast + stone coal). If any part of the combination is itself new, that further supports the novelty of the whole combination. Examples and citations are given (Lister v. Leather, McCall v. Rintt, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: New application (new mode of applying a known thing) can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A new mode of applying a known thing may be the subject of a patent provided some ingenuity and novelty are exhibited in the mode of making that application, and the application is attended by some useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Watt's insulating of the cylinder; Forsyth's use of fulminating compounds to discharge firearms; Derosne's improved charcoal filtering for sugar — in each the application of known materials/methods in a novel mode that yields a practical advantage was upheld. The jury's factual finding of novelty/usefulness supports validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope and specificity: avoid claiming the 'principle' or every possible shape
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee must not claim the abstract principle or claim every shape/variation; claims must be specific to a mode or machine embodying the principle. If a claim is effectively for a principle (e.g., 'every shape of vessel'), it will be treated as a principle and not allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish acceptable claims (specific mechanical embodiments or modes) from unacceptable sweeping claims. Example: Baron Alderson's comment in the Neilson case: 'Then I think that is a principle, if you claim every shape. If you claim a specific shape, ... then I can understand it.' Overbroad claiming is an anti-pattern that risks invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability may depend on whether the monopoly is void by statute or permitted by common law (procedural/legal assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the validity of a monopoly (patent) is questioned, first consider whether it is rendered void by statute; if not, consider whether it is a privilege permitted by the common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sets the procedural/legal framework for validity challenges: statutory prohibitions (e.g., statutes against monopolies) and common-law permissibility determine whether a royal grant/patent is enforceable. The treatise notes that patentees derive their monopoly through Crown prerogative preserved by statute provisos, but the courts ultimately judge validity.
